text: In 1924, the world's biggest lightbulb makers made a secret deal. Make the bulb... worse.
Companies from Germany, the Netherlands, France, Britain and Japan, plus an American giant working through its overseas arms.
Back then, a good bulb could burn up to two thousand hours.
The new rule: one thousand. Max.
Every factory mailed sample bulbs to a lab in Switzerland.
Bulb lasted too long? The factory paid a fine.
And it worked. Real bulb life dropped by about a third.
Here's the twist: bulbs got cheaper to make, but prices barely moved.
Because every bulb that burns out is a bulb you buy again.
The deal only died in 1940, when war tore it apart. Your bulb didn't just burn out. It was scheduled to.
